group.passage:
When astronauts keep exploring mysteries in outer space, their physical conditions while in orbit may actually benefit medical science on the ground.
Surprisingly, astronauts often complain about kidney stones when they’re returning to Earth. Kidney stones are salt or mineral deposits in kidneys, delivering paralyzing pain to sufferers if not treated in time. Most of us understand that one’s weight and diet play a crucial role in whether one comes down with the painful condition. However, astronauts are supposedly physically and mentally fit, with their diet and daily routine carefully monitored by specialized teams. When astronauts develop kidney stones while in space, they usually have no choice but to <u>abort</u> their mission because of the unbearable pain and lack of medical personnel onboard.
Tasked to look into the causes and possible treatment of kidney stones in astronauts, a team headed by Dr. Stephen Walsh sent mice aboard the International Space Station, and exposed the control group to conditions similar to those in space. They came to the conclusion that gamma radiation and the weightless environment are responsible for the painful condition. The former affects kidney cells and hence the transport and absorption of fat and proteins, while the latter gives rise to certain bacterial growth.
Hopefully, not only will further research ensure the success of future space missions but it will be one key missing puzzle piece in our ambition of space travel. The general public prone to kidney stones will probably benefit as well. Given the implications of cosmic radiation in kidney stones, patients undergoing radiotherapy for cancer may also be able to avoid damaging healthy tissues during treatment. With devoted teams and concerted effort, we can definitely come up with a solution soon.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the second paragraph?

options.A: People may not associate astronauts with kidney stones in the first place.
options.B: Astronauts usually recover from kidney stones faster than most of us do.
options.C: Living in space is believed to be difficult even for astronauts.
options.D: Kidney stones will not cause much trouble in the early stages.

questions.stem: Which of the underlined words below is the closest in meaning to the word “abort” in the second paragraph?

options.A: “We are supposed to conduct further research so that we can <u>strengthen</u> our stance with more convincing arguments.”
options.B: “She decided to <u>terminate</u> her contract with her company, and to work for another start-up that guarantees more benefits.”
options.C: “I find it impossible to <u>condone</u> her criminal behavior. A lot of people are suffering needlessly because of her.”
options.D: “I believe they have done everything possible to <u>contain</u> the disease. We must not blame them for the new confirmed cases.”

questions.stem: What can we know from Dr. Stephen Walsh’s research on kidney stones?

options.A: Kidney stones can usually be treated with medication and surgery.
options.B: We must watch what we eat if we’re worried about having kidney stones.
options.C: Those who are overweight are more likely to have kidney stones.
options.D: There is more than one cause of kidney stones in astronauts.
